description:
Elizabeth Holmes promised to run hundreds of medical tests from a single drop of blood. Investors valued her company at 9 billion dollars. There was only one problem: the machine never really worked.

This is the story of Theranos, the Silicon Valley startup that fooled billionaires, former secretaries of state, a giant pharmacy chain and millions of patients, until a young employee and a journalist decided to tell the truth.

• A 19-year-old dropout with a huge idea
• The black turtleneck and the deep voice
• The most powerful board in Silicon Valley
• The whistleblowers who risked everything
• From 9 billion dollars to a prison cell

segments.text: Imagine a machine the size of a printer that could run hundreds of medical tests from a single drop of blood taken from your finger. No needles in your arm, no waiting days for results, a fraction of the price. In 2014, investors believed this machine existed, and they valued the company that built it at around 9 billion dollars. The founder became the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world. There was just one problem. The machine did not work.

The founder was Elizabeth Holmes. In 2003, at just 19 years old, she dropped out of Stanford University to start a company. She said she was afraid of needles, and she wanted to change healthcare forever. She called the company Theranos, a mix of the words therapy and diagnosis. Her idea was beautiful. Blood testing is a huge industry, and if you could make it cheap, fast and painless, you could save lives and make a fortune at the same time.

Holmes was incredibly good at one thing: convincing people. She raised money from some of the richest families in America. She built a board of directors that looked like a history book. Former Secretary of State George Shultz. Former Secretary of State Henry Kissinger. Later, General James Mattis, who would become Secretary of Defense. Famous names, powerful names. But notice something. Almost none of them were experts in blood testing.

She also built an image. She wore black turtlenecks, just like Steve Jobs. She spoke in a very deep voice, which former employees later said was not always her natural voice. She rarely blinked in interviews. Magazines put her on their covers. Everybody wanted to believe that the next Steve Jobs was a young woman who was going to revolutionize medicine. And that desire to believe is exactly what made the fraud possible.

Inside the company, the reality was very different. The device, called the Edison, could only run a small number of tests, and the results were often unreliable. So what did Theranos do? According to prosecutors and former employees, it quietly ran many of the tests on commercial machines bought from other companies, sometimes modified to work with tiny samples. The public was told everything was done on Theranos technology. It was not.

And then came the moment that changed everything. In 2013, Theranos signed a deal with Walgreens, one of the biggest pharmacy chains in the United States. Theranos wellness centers opened inside Walgreens stores in Arizona and California. Real patients, real blood, real medical decisions. People were getting results about cholesterol, diabetes and even cancer markers from a system that the company's own employees did not trust. But that was not the most shocking part.

Walgreens was not the only giant that fell for it. The supermarket chain Safeway also signed a deal and reportedly spent around 350 million dollars building clinics inside its stores, ready for Theranos testing. The clinics were built. The testing never really arrived. And even the military got involved. General Mattis wanted to test the device on the battlefield in Afghanistan, but army officials who looked at the technology raised doubts, and it never happened. Every time an expert looked closely, something did not add up.

The most shocking part was how the company kept its secrets. Employees were watched closely. Departments were separated so that nobody saw the full picture. Workers who asked too many questions were pushed out or fired. Lawyers threatened people who spoke up. And the man who helped Holmes run all of this was Sunny Balwani, the company's president and chief operating officer, who was also, secretly, her romantic partner.

Meanwhile, the money kept flowing. In 2014, Theranos was valued at around 9 billion dollars. Holmes owned about half of it, which gave her a paper fortune of roughly 4.5 billion dollars. She was on the Forbes list of the richest Americans. And all of that value was built on a technology that almost no outsider had ever tested. If you like these stories about how the biggest companies rise and fall, subscribe, because there are many more coming.

Now let's talk about the people who stopped her. One of them was a young employee named Tyler Shultz. And yes, the surname is not a coincidence. He was the grandson of George Shultz, the former Secretary of State sitting on Theranos's board. Tyler saw that the tests were failing quality checks and that data was being manipulated. He told his grandfather. His grandfather, at first, believed Holmes instead of him.

Another employee, a young lab worker called Erika Cheung, saw the same problems. She reported them to regulators. Both of them faced enormous pressure. Tyler Shultz later said the company's lawyers followed him and threatened him with lawsuits, and his family spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on legal fees. They were in their twenties, fighting a 9 billion dollar company with the most powerful board in Silicon Valley.

Then, a journalist enters the story. John Carreyrou, an investigative reporter at the Wall Street Journal, received a tip about Theranos. He started talking to former employees. Theranos tried everything to stop him. Its lawyers pressured sources and even tried to stop the article before publication. But in October 2015, the Wall Street Journal published the story. And from that moment, the whole thing started to collapse.

Regulators inspected the laboratory and found serious problems. Theranos had to void years of blood test results, tens of thousands of them. Walgreens ended the partnership. In 2016, Forbes changed its estimate of Holmes's fortune from 4.5 billion dollars to exactly zero. In 2018, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged Holmes and Balwani with what it called a massive fraud, and later that year Theranos shut down for good.

The criminal trial came later. In January 2022, a jury found Elizabeth Holmes guilty of defrauding investors. She was sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison. Sunny Balwani was convicted on all charges in a separate trial and received an even longer sentence, nearly 13 years. In 2023, the woman who had been on magazine covers as the next Steve Jobs reported to a prison in Texas.

So how did so many smart people get fooled? The investors did not ask for independent tests, because everybody else had already invested. The board members trusted her charm and each other's names. The media loved the story too much to question it. Everyone assumed that someone else had checked. Nobody really had. The people who finally checked were a 22 year old employee, a lab worker and a newspaper reporter.

There is a famous phrase in Silicon Valley: fake it till you make it. It works when you are building software and the product is a little late. But when the product is a medical test, faking it means real people making real decisions about their health based on wrong results. Theranos is the story of what happens when a good idea meets unlimited money and nobody is allowed to say no.

And the craziest part? The original idea was not stupid. Cheaper and easier blood testing is still a real goal that many scientists are working on today. Theranos did not fail because the dream was impossible. It failed because it pretended the dream had already come true. So tell me in the comments: who do you think deserves the most blame? Holmes, the investors, or the famous board members who never checked?

segments.text: This machine made a 19 year old dropout worth 4.5 billion dollars. Elizabeth Holmes said it could run hundreds of tests from one drop of blood. Her board included two former secretaries of state. Walgreens put it in its stores. But inside the company, many tests were secretly run on other companies' machines. A 22 year old employee blew the whistle, a journalist published the story, and Holmes went from billionaire to prison. The full story is on the channel.
